title: Hot and cold
text: Pattern fourteen: hot fields and cold fields. A scan that needs eighteen bytes per order shouldn't drag in a hundred and twelve. Here's the layout you get by default, and the one a hot loop wants.

title: The general version
text: The task: total the open bid quantity at or above a price, across every resting order. The general version keeps one rich Order struct: two strings, an id, two timestamps, price, quantity and four flags, 112 bytes. The scan is a clear loop with one if. It's a good design for an order store, and most reviews would approve it.

title: What it costs
text: Here are four orders, back to back, with the bytes the scan needs in green. But the core never loads a field: it loads whole 64-byte cache lines. The scan reads five of every seven lines, about 80 bytes per order, and the prefetcher streams in the rest. A million orders is 117 megabytes per scan, far beyond the 2 megabyte L2, so most lines come from far away. And the strings and timestamps that ride along evict the lines you'll need next.

title: The hot path version
text: The hot path version lays data out by how it's read. Each field the scan needs becomes its own array: price, quantity, and one precomputed byte, live bid. Strings, timestamps and the other flags move to a cold store, at the same index. The loop now reads only bytes it uses: seventeen per order, packed densely in every line. The filter becomes a mask, so random order flow can't cause mispredicts. The price of the split: live bid must be updated on every fill and cancel.

title: Measured
text: Measured on a shared 4 vCPU cloud VM, each scan pinned to one core, median of five runs. Bytes moved per order: 112 for the fat struct, 24 for a hot and cold split, and 17 for struct of arrays. With a million orders, the general version takes about 24 nanoseconds per order on this busy box, and struct of arrays takes 0.77. Give the fat struct the same branchless body, and it still takes 17, so this is layout, not branches. A hot and cold split, with one 24-byte hot struct, gets 1.1. At 8 million orders, everything streams from memory, and the gap settles near the byte ratio: 21 against 2.8 nanoseconds, about seven times. At one million it's bigger, because the 18 megabytes of hot arrays stay in cache, and the 117 megabytes of structs don't.

title: The rule
text: One rich struct isn't wrong. When you touch the whole order, a new order, an amend, a fill report, keep it together. When a hot loop scans a few fields across many orders, split those fields out. The cost is bookkeeping: one index, kept in sync on every state change. And measure bytes per element and the working set against your caches, not just nanoseconds. The rule: lay data out by how the hot loop reads it, not by what it's called.
